| Payment | Card or debit by default; invoicing available at Verda's discretion; no cryptocurrency documented | Crypto only — USDT (TRC-20/ERC-20), BTC, XMR, LTC, ETH, TRX, SOL |
| Identity | No KYC clause in the Terms and Conditions; billing name, email, phone and address required to set up an account | Email + password. No KYC, no card, no stored IP addresses |
| Free credit | None advertised on the current pricing or company pages | None — every hour is ≥30% under the market median instead |
| Cheaper tier | Spot tier at roughly −50% versus on-demand; reserved capacity from a 1-month minimum term | Interruptible flat −50% (no auction) · reserved −35% (3+ months) |
| Regions | 3 own-operated sites: Helsinki ×2 (Finland), Reykjanesbaer ×1 (Iceland); a fourth (Akaa, Finland) and international offices announced, none live yet | 32 regions on 5 continents, verified datacenters only |
| Minimums | None for pay-as-you-go; reserved capacity starts at 1 month | None — 1× to 8× GPUs at the same per-GPU price |
| Storage | $0.20/GiB/month NVMe | $0.08/GB/month NVMe, volumes survive instances |
| Egress | Not published on Verda's pricing or FAQ pages | $0.01/GB in and out, every region |
| Access | Self-serve console and API, no sales call for the instances listed above | Containers or full KVM VMs, SSH, Jupyter, REST API, CLI, Python SDK |

results.title: European GPU Clouds: 8 Alternatives to AWS and Azure ...
results.author: Mélanie Dallé
highlights:
- Scaleway (France, Iliad group): H100 PCIe, H100 SXM, L40S and L4 behind managed Kubernetes (Kapsule) with public per-hour pricing. Best for EU teams that want a full cloud and GPUs in one console.
- OVHcloud (France): H100, A100, L40S single cards plus 8xH200 nodes, managed Kubernetes (MKS), free egress and public pricing. Best for the widest published EU GPU catalogue.
- Nscale: an AI-first cloud running hydro-powered data centres in Glomfjord, Norway (EEA), with H100, H200 and GB200/GB300-class systems sold by quote. Best for large committed training clusters.
- Verda (formerly DataCrunch, Finland): public on-demand and spot pricing for H100, H200, B200 and GB300. Best for price-sensitive training and fine-tuning with transparent rates.
- Hetzner (Germany): monthly dedicated GPU servers (NVIDIA RTX 4000 SFF Ada, RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell), not hourly cloud. Best for cheap, steady inference you can commit to monthly.
- IONOS (Germany, United Internet): NVIDIA H200 cloud VMs at a flat per-GPU-hour rate, EU hosting and ISO 27001. Best for regulated EU workloads that want a simple H200 rate.
- Exoscale (Austria, A1 Group): GPU families around NVIDIA A40, A30, V100 and RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell across Frankfurt, Vienna, Geneva and Zagreb. Best for compliance-heavy EU workloads that do not need H100 or H200.
- Vast.ai and RunPod (GPU marketplaces): H100 SXM and A100 by the hour at the cheapest headline rates, where European hosting, DPA coverage and uptime depend on the individual host you rent from. Best for burst and experimentation, not regulated production.

...

On published EU on-demand list prices checked in September 2026, AWS charges roughly $7.36 per H100 GPU-hour (p5.48xlarge at $58.89/hour for 8 GPUs in eu-north-1, Stockholm) and Azure roughly $15.98 per H100 GPU-hour (ND96isr H100 v5 at $127.82/hour for 8 GPUs in West Europe). European specialists list H100 far below both, with Scaleway around EUR 2.87, OVHcloud at $2.99 and Verda at $3.25 per GPU-hour, and the Vast.ai/RunPod marketplace tier dips lower still at the cost of predictable quality. Read marketplace rates as a floor, not a guarantee.

results.title: NVIDIA's Vera Rubin & Blackwell GPU Server Prices Could Soar By As Much As 17% As Memory Prices Bite, Say Reports
results.author: Ramish Zafar
highlights:
Chip designer NVIDIA Corporation might increase the prices of its server products by at least 15% suggest multiple media reports. NVIDIA, like other AI and non-AI technology companies, is facing the heat from the tight memory market, which has led to memory chips becoming one of the most expensive components of a technology product. According to the details, servers shipped with NVIDIA's Blackwell and Rubin products will experience the price hike and they are expected to be available in the market next year.

...

Throughout 2026, multiple reports have suggested that both NVIDIA and AMD have had to raise the prices of their graphics processing units (GPUs). A report in late-July suggested that NVIDIA had hiked its GPU prices for the third time in 2026, with the hikes ranging between 20% to 30%. According to the details, these price hikes were on consumer-facing chip products, and they came on top of a 10% to 15% hike in January. 

In August, the media price of an NVIDIA RTX 5060 Ti 16GB GPU had jumped by 88% over its launch price to $805. The report came after NVIDIA and AMD's board partners increased the prices of the RTX 50 and Radeon RX 9000 Series products by 20%. 

The price hikes for the GPUs come as memory shortages have led to DDR4 prices jumping by as much as 50% in the third quarter of 2026. Memory chip manufacturers have prioritized their production lines for HBM memory, typically used in AI chips, and the resulting shortage has led to a recalibration all over the market. 

Now, reports from Bloomberg and The Information suggest that NVIDIA might increase its server prices by as much as 15% to 17%. The 15% figure comes courtesy of Bloomberg. It claims that some of NVIDIA's customers have been informed of the price hikes. The price hikes are expected to go into effect with systems shipped in 2027, and they will involve products relying on the Vera Rubin and the Blackwell GPU chips. Bloomberg's sources added that the price hikes will depend on the chips being used and the amount of memory they carry. 

The Information makes similar claims. It shares that servers with the Grace Blackwell 300 and Vera Rubin 200 chips that will be delivered next year will be impacted by the change. The report adds that the price hikes could mean that the cost of a one-gigawatt data center could jump by at least $5 billion, primarily due to the higher memory chip prices. The Information also outlines that the cost of these hikes could be passed by the cloud system operators to their customers.
